question: Sheep pox and goat pox have remained endemic in Greece since 2023, with continuous outbreaks mainly found in Macedonia and Thrace. Despite containment measures and the mass killing of herds, the disease continues to spread. This has severe repercussions for livestock farming, the rural economy and social cohesion in the affected areas.

DG SANTE’s reports (16 May 2025) highlight the insufficient administrative capacity of the Greek authorities, the difficulties in monitoring restricted zones and the risk of further spread. In accordance with Article 12 of Regulation (EU) 2020/687 and Article 69 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429, Member States may postpone the killing of listed animals and implement a vaccination plan.

Nevertheless, the Greek Government argues that sheep pox and goat pox vaccines are not authorised, citing national legislation which still sets out the killing of animals as a key measure. Conversely, the European Commission and DG SANTE explicitly refer to vaccination strategies and making use of the European vaccine bank for category A diseases. In view of the above, can the Commission say: 1.
Are authorised sheep pox and goat pox vaccines available, and if so, in what quantities?
What measures will be taken to ensure that Greece complies with EU law permitting vaccination as an alternative to killing?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.1.2026) Currently there is no approved sheep and goat pox (SGP) vaccine in the EU. Nonetheless, the Veterinary Medicinal Products Regulation1 allows Member States’ competent authorities to use a vaccine not authorised within the Union. An EU SGP vaccine bank is in place and can ship vaccines free of charge to a requiring Member State (no request received to date).

Control measures at EU level for SGP are laid down in Regulation (EU) 2016/4292 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/6873. These measures include the immediate killing of kept animals of listed species in an affected establishment and the demarcation of restricted zones around the outbreaks.

These measures are mandatory, and vaccination, should Greece decide to vaccinate, can only be applied in addition to them, not as an alternative. In addition, if Greece decides to vaccinate, it must submit a vaccination plan compliant with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/3614.

Then, the Commission may adopt a riskbased and proportionate plan establishing the necessary risk-mitigating measures, consistent with the standards of the World Organisation for Animal Health5 and the treatments foreseen under Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

Furthermore, the Commission continuously monitors and evaluates the implementation of EU rules through audits, ensuring they remain risk-based, proportionate and fully compliant with the EU legal framework, while safeguarding both animal health and the internal market.
